title_en: Beijing Wansheng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office, Third Party: Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. — administrative dispute over invalidation of invention patent right
ruling_gist_en: 1. A compound claim drafted in Markush format has always been regarded as a structural expression rather than a functional expression. The Markush claim defines alternative interchangeable elements, rather than separate claims, and shall comply with the provisions on unity of invention under the Patent Law and the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law. A Markush claim shall be deemed as a collection of Markush elements, rather than a collection of numerous compounds, and shall be understood as a class of compounds having common properties and effects. 2. Strict restrictions must be imposed on the amendment of a Markush claim during the invalidation proceedings. The principle for allowing amendment of a Markush claim should be that no amendment may result in the creation of a class or a single compound with new properties and effects, while specific circumstances of individual cases shall also be fully considered. 3. The determination of inventiveness of a Markush claim shall follow the basic method for determining inventiveness, i.e., the 'three-step method' prescribed in the Patent Examination Guidelines. Unexpected technical effect is an auxiliary factor in the determination of inventiveness, and generally it should not be applied directly across the 'three-step method' to determine whether a patent application is inventive.

full_text_en:
Beijing Wansheng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. v.

Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office,

Third Party: Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. — Administrative Dispute over Invalidation of Invention Patent Right

【Ruling Summary】

1. A compound claim drafted in Markush format has always been regarded as an expression of a structural formula rather than a functional expression. A Markush claim defines a group of alternative elements, not individual claims, and shall comply with the provisions of the Patent Law and the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law regarding unity of invention. A Markush claim shall be deemed as a collection of Markush elements, not a collection of numerous compounds, and shall be understood as a class of compounds having common properties and effects. 2. In the invalidation stage, amendments to a Markush claim must be strictly limited. The principle for permitting amendments to a Markush claim should be that no new class of compounds or individual compound with new properties and effects may be created as a result of the amendment. However, case-specific factors must also be fully considered. 3. The determination of inventiveness of a Markush claim shall follow the basic method for determining inventiveness, i.e., the "three-step method" stipulated in the Patent Examination Guidelines. An unexpected technical effect is an auxiliary factor in the determination of inventiveness. It is generally inappropriate to jump over the "three-step method" and directly apply the presence of an unexpected technical effect to determine whether a patent application possesses inventiveness.

Administrative Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2016) Zui Gao Fa Xing Zai No. 41

Applicant for Retrial (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office. Domicile: Floors 10-12, Yin'gu Building, No. 9, Beisihuan West Road, Haidian District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Ge Shu, Deputy Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Liu Hongzun, Examiner of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Liu Xinlei, Examiner of the Board.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Beijing Wansheng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 8, Guangyuan East Street, Tongzhou Industrial Development Zone, Tongzhou District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Huang He, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Huang Zexiong, Patent Agent of Beijing BangXinYang Patent & Trademark Agency Co., Ltd.

Agent ad litem: Hou Haiyan, Patent Agent of Beijing BangXinYang Patent & Trademark Agency Co., Ltd.

Third Party at First Instance: Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. Domicile: 5-1, Nihonbashi Honcho 3-chome, Chuo-ku, Tokyo, Japan.

Legal Representative: Nakayama Joji, Representative Director and President.

Agent ad litem: Chen Wenping, Lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Mao Jin, Lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

The applicant for retrial, the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board), being dissatisfied with the administrative judgment (2012) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 833 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Beijing High People's Court) in the case of the administrative dispute over invalidation of invention patent right between the respondent Beijing Wansheng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Wansheng Company) and the third party at first and second instances, Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd., applied to this Court for retrial. This Court rendered the administrative ruling (2014) Zhi Xing Zi No. 56 on December 23, 2015, deciding to bring this case for retrial. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and opened a court session to hear this case. Agents ad litem of the Patent Reexamination Board, Liu Hongzun and Liu Xinlei, agents ad litem of Wansheng Pharmaceutical, Huang Zexiong and Hou Haiyan, and agents ad litem of Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd., Chen Wenping and Mao Jin, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The case is now concluded.

Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. is the patentee of the invention patent titled "Method for Preparing a Pharmaceutical Composition for Treating or Preventing Hypertension," patent number 97126347.7 (hereinafter referred to as the patent-in-suit). On April 23, 2010, Wansheng Company filed a request for invalidation of the patent-in-suit with the Patent Reexamination Board. On April 1, 2011, the Patent Reexamination Board issued the Invalidation Request Examination Decision No. 16266 (hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 16266), maintaining the validity of the patent-in-suit in its entirety. Dissatisfied with Decision No. 16266, Wansheng Company initiated an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court.

The court of first instance found through trial: The case concerns invention patent No. 97126347.7, titled "Method for Preparing a Pharmaceutical Composition for Treating or Preventing Hypertension," which was granted and published by the State Intellectual Property Office on September 24, 2003, with a filing date of February 21, 1992. The patentee is Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. The claims as granted and published for the patent-in-suit are as follows:

"1. A method for preparing a pharmaceutical composition for treating or preventing hypertension, comprising mixing an antihypertensive agent with a pharmaceutically acceptable carrier or diluent, wherein the antihypertensive agent is at least one compound of formula (I) as shown below or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt or ester thereof,

wherein:

R1 represents an alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms;

R2 and R3 are the same or different and each represents an alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms;

R4 represents: a hydrogen atom; or an alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms:

R5 represents a carboxyl group, a group of formula COOR5a, or a group of formula -CONR8R9, wherein R8 and R9 are the same or different and each represents: a hydrogen atom; an unsubstituted alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms; a substituted alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms, wherein the alkyl group is substituted by a carboxyl group or an alkoxycarbonyl group whose alkyl moiety has 1 to 6 carbon atoms; or R8 and R9 together represent a substituted alkylene group having 2 to 6 carbon atoms, wherein the alkylene group is substituted by an alkoxycarbonyl group whose alkyl moiety has 1 to 6 carbon atoms;

and wherein R5a represents:

an alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms;

an alkanoyloxyalkyl group, wherein the alkanoyl moiety and the alkyl moiety each have 1 to 6 carbon atoms;

an alkoxycarbonyloxyalkyl group, wherein the alkoxy moiety and the alkyl moiety each have 1 to 6 carbon atoms;

(5-methyl-2-oxo-1,3-dioxol-4-yl)methyl; or 2-benzo[c]furanonyl;

R6 represents a hydrogen atom; and R7 represents a carboxyl group or a tetrazol-5-yl group."

The specification of the patent-in-suit records: We have discovered that a limited class of 1-(biphenylmethyl)-imidazole-5-carboxylic acid derivatives possess excellent AII receptor antagonist activity, thereby being useful as antihypertensive drugs and for the treatment and prevention of cardiac diseases. To this end, one object of the invention is to provide a series of new 1-(biphenylmethyl)-imidazole-5-carboxylic acid derivatives. Pages 107-108 of the specification of the patent-in-suit record the activity data for a number of specific (test) compounds of formula (I) as defined in claim 1, which showed unexpected effects compared to Compound A of the prior art.

With respect to the patent-in-suit, Wansheng Company filed a request for invalidation with the Patent Reexamination Board on April 23, 2010, on the grounds that claim 1 of the patent-in-suit did not comply with Article 22(3) of the Patent Law, Article 26(4) of the Patent Law, and Rule 20(1) of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law. Simultaneously, Wansheng Company submitted the following evidence, including:

Evidence 1: European Patent Application No. EP0324377A2, with a publication date of July 19, 1989, copy of 271 pages, and a Chinese translation of pages 1, 2 (second-to-last line) to 15 (second-to-last line), totaling 15 pages of translation. Page 15 of the translation records: The most preferred compounds for antihypertensive activity are the following new compounds and their pharmaceutically acceptable salts. The second preferred compound is the compound of Example 329 of Evidence 1: 2-propyl-1-[(2'-(1H-tetrazol-5-yl)biphenyl-4-yl)methyl]imidazole-4,5-dicarboxylic acid; the third compound is the compound of Example 265C of Evidence 1: 2-propyl-4-pentafluoroethyl-1-[(2'-(1H-tetrazol-5-yl)biphenyl-4-yl)methyl]imidazole-5-carboxylic acid. Pages 4-8 of the Chinese translation of Evidence 1 define multiple optional substituents for R1, R2, R3, R6, R7, and R8 in the compound of formula (I) of Evidence 1, and also define multiple optional substituents for R9 to R32 related to the substituents R1, R2, R3, R6, R7, and R8.

On August 30, 2010, Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. filed its observations regarding the invalidation request, and simultaneously amended its claims, including: deleting the words "or ester" from "or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt or ester" in claim 1; deleting "an alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms" under the definition of R4 in claim 1; deleting from the definition of R5 in claim 1 all technical solutions other than the carboxyl group and the group of formula COOR5a (wherein R5a is (5-methyl-2-oxo-1,3-dioxol-4-yl)methyl).

Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. argued that: In the amended claim 1, the expression "or ester" had been deleted, and thus the grounds for invalidation based on Article 26(4) of the Patent Law and Rule 20(1) of the Implementing Regulations could no longer be sustained. Evidence 1 did not disclose what Wansheng Company referred to as the "closest compound." The substituent at the 4-position of the imidazole ring of the patented compound was not similar or close to that of Evidence 1, and there was no evidence that they had the same or similar effects. Evidence 1 did not teach that the patented compound had significantly better antihypertensive activity than Evidence 1.

On January 12, 2011, the Patent Reexamination Board conducted an oral hearing. During the oral hearing, the following facts were confirmed:

(1) The Patent Reexamination Board informed Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. that, regarding the amended text submitted on August 30, 2010, the amendment deleting "or ester" from claim 1 was accepted, but the remaining amendments did not comply with the relevant provisions of Rule 68 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law, and thus the amended text was not accepted. Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. and Wansheng Company had no objection to this.

Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. expressly stated that it would only delete "or ester" from claim 1 and would submit the amended text within three days after the hearing. Wansheng Company confirmed that if Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. deleted "or ester" from claim 1, it would withdraw the grounds for invalidation based on Article 26(4) of the Patent Law and Rule 20(1) of the Implementing Regulations; otherwise, it would insist on the above grounds for invalidation.

(2) Wansheng Company admitted that the specific compounds or generic definitions in Evidence 1 mentioned in its request were all selected from the compound of formula (I) of Evidence 1 and were not explicitly recorded in Evidence 1; furthermore, Wansheng Company admitted that there was no evidence in this case to prove the common general knowledge described on page 5 of the request.

(3) Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. acknowledged that the object of the invention or the achieved technical effect of the patent-in-suit was recorded in the third paragraph on page 2 of the specification of the patent-in-suit, and Wansheng Company had no objection to this.

On January 14, 2011, Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. submitted a statement of opinions and replacement pages for the amended claims, wherein it deleted "or ester" from claim 1.

On February 1, 2011, the Patent Reexamination Board forwarded the above documents to Wansheng Company, requesting a response within a specified period. Wansheng Company raised no objections within the specified period. On April 1, 2011, the Patent Reexamination Board issued Decision No. 16266, finding that: (I) Basis for Examination. The text on which this decision is based is: claim 1 submitted by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. on January 14, 2011, pages 1-195 of the specification as granted and published, and the abstract of the specification. (II) Regarding Article 22(3) of the Patent Law. Comparing the compound of formula (I) of claim 1 with the compound of formula (I) of Evidence 1, the differences lie in the following: First, the substituents defined for R5 at the 5-position of the imidazole ring and R2R3(OR4) at the 4-position of the imidazole ring in claim 1 of the patent-in-suit are different from the substituents defined for R7 and R8, which can be at the 4- and 5-positions of the imidazole ring in Evidence 1; second, the definition ranges of R1, R6, and R7 in the compound of formula (I) of the patent-in-suit, the number of CH2 groups connecting the imidazole ring and the benzene ring, and the definition ranges of substituents on the benzene ring are different from those of the compound of formula (I) of Evidence 1. The compound of formula (I) of Evidence 1 encompasses a vastly larger number of compounds.

First, from the content disclosed in Evidence 1, it can be seen that the compound of formula (I) of Evidence 1 not only includes multiple substituent cases defined by R1, R2, R3, R6, R7, and R8, but also the optional substituents R9 to 32 related to these substituents define an even greater number of compounds of formula (I) of Evidence 1. Evidence 1 neither discloses the compound of structure I specifically defined in claim 1 of the patent-in-suit nor the specific compound described by Wansheng Company in its request; moreover, among the multiple substitution possibilities for the 4-position substituent of the imidazole ring, i.e., the numerous substituent options defined by R7 and R8, there is even no record that the 4-position of the imidazole ring of the generic compound can be substituted by a hydroxy-branched alkyl group or an alkoxy-branched alkyl group. Second, Evidence 1 does not disclose, and Wansheng Company has no evidence to prove, that the alkyl group at the 4-position of the imidazole ring in the compound of formula (I) of Evidence 1 can be interchanged with an alkoxy-branched alkyl group or a hydroxy-branched alkyl group, nor does it disclose that the effects after such interchange are the same or similar. Therefore, a person skilled in the art, based on the content disclosed in Evidence 1, would need to exercise inventive effort to select and arrive at the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent-in-suit. The technical solution of claim 1 is not obvious in light of Evidence 1. Third, the patent-in-suit not only records activity data for a number of specific compounds of the formula (I), but also demonstrates that the compounds in the patent-in-suit have unexpected effects compared to the closest compound A of the background technology (see pages 1, 107, and 108 of the specification of the patent-in-suit) and are effective as antihypertensive drugs. Moreover, patent application documents do not generally need to provide experimental data comparing all compounds of the patent with all compounds of the prior art. As stated above, a person skilled in the art could not derive a technical suggestion for the compound of formula (I) of the patent-in-suit from the content of Evidence 1. Therefore, the patent-in-suit possesses inventiveness over Evidence 1 and complies with Article 22(3) of the Patent Law.

For the same reasons, the compound allegedly disclosed in Evidence 1 where R1 represents an optionally substituted phenyl group connected at the 4-position, with the substitution site at the 5-position, R13 is a 4-azolyl group, R2 represents hydrogen, R3 represents hydrogen; R6 represents a straight-chain propyl group; R7 represents a branched-chain butyl group; R8 represents a carboxyl group, as well as the specific compound structure submitted by Wansheng Company during the hearing differing only in the 4-position substituent of the imidazole ring, are not technical solutions disclosed in Evidence 1. Wansheng Company also admitted that Evidence 1 did not disclose the above generic formula and specific compounds. Therefore, these compounds cannot constitute the closest prior art for evaluating the inventiveness of the patent-in-suit.

Furthermore, comparing the structures of the compounds of Examples 329 and 265C disclosed on page 15 of the Chinese translation of Evidence 1 with the compound of claim 1 of the patent-in-suit, the differences are that the 4-position substituents of the imidazole ring in the compounds of Examples 329 and 265C of Evidence 1 are C2F5 and COOH groups, respectively, while the 4-position substituent of the imidazole ring in the compound of claim 1 of the patent-in-suit is a substituent R2R3(OR4) as defined, i.e., a hydroxy-branched alkyl group or an alkoxy-branched alkyl group. However, the 4-position substituents C2F5 and COOH of the imidazole ring in the above compounds of Evidence 1 are different from the hydroxy-branched alkyl group or alkoxy-branched alkyl group defined in the patent-in-suit. Moreover, Evidence 1 does not even record in its definition of the multiple substituent options for the 4-position of the imidazole ring that this position can be selected as a hydroxy-branched alkyl group or an alkoxy-branched alkyl group. Evidence 1 also does not disclose that the 4-position substituents C2F5 or COOH of the imidazole ring can be replaced by a hydroxy-branched alkyl group or an alkoxy-branched alkyl group. Thus, the above content of Evidence 1 provides no suggestion that the 4-position of the imidazole ring could be a hydroxy-branched alkyl group or an alkoxy-branched alkyl group. At the same time, Wansheng Company did not provide evidence proving that common technical knowledge existed in the prior art indicating that the 4-position of the imidazole ring in Examples 329 and 265C of Evidence 1 could be replaced by the hydroxy-branched alkyl group or alkoxy-branched alkyl group of the patent-in-suit, nor did it prove that the compound after replacement possesses the described activity or effect. Therefore, claim 1 of the patent-in-suit is non-obvious in light of Evidence 1 and possesses inventiveness, complying with Article 22(3) of the Patent Law.

In summary, the Patent Reexamination Board issued Examination Decision No. 16266, maintaining the validity of the patent-in-suit in its entirety based on the amended text submitted by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. on January 14, 2011.

It is further found that during the patent grant procedure of the patent-in-suit, the substantive examination department of the State Intellectual Property Office once considered that the patent application had a very similar structure to Annex 1 of this case and both had antihypertensive activity, thus lacking inventiveness, and requested the patent applicant to provide experimental data. The patent applicant subsequently provided experimental data comparing the application with Annex 1. In these data, the applicant argued that, comparing the compounds of Examples 251A, 265A, 265C, 329, and 335 of Document 1 (the counterpart of Annex 1), where R2 was 2-propyl, with the compounds of Examples 19 and 24 of the application, where R2 was also 2-propyl, the ID50 values of the compounds of Document 1 (being 0.04, 0.02, 0.1, 0.031, and 1.7, respectively) were 5, 2.5, 12.5, 3.88, 212.5 times and 2.86, 1.43, 7.14, 2.21, 121.43 times higher than the ID50 values of the compounds of the application (being 0.008 and 0.014, respectively). Thus, the compounds of the application were clearly superior to the compounds of Document 1. It was evident that the compounds of the application, containing a tert-butanol group at the 4-position of the imidazole ring, exhibited surprisingly high activity.

During the second instance of this case, based on the amended claims of Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd., the ID50 data for some test compounds disclosed in Table 7 of the specification of the patent-in-suit, and the ID50 data for Example 329 of Evidence 1 recorded in the statement of opinions submitted by the patent applicant to the substantive examination department of the State Intellectual Property Office, the following table can be derived:

The above facts are supported by Decision No. 16266, Evidence 1, patent examination documents, and statements of the parties.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held that the designation of the type of the invalidation decision on the front page of Decision No. 16266 as "maintaining the patent right valid" can only be understood as maintaining the patent right valid on the basis of the amended text submitted by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. on January 14, 2011, rather than maintaining the patent right valid on the basis of the claim text at the time of patent grant. Decision No. 16266 did not contain any error in fact finding. Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd.'s deletion of the Markush elements from the Markush claim does not directly equate to the deletion of parallel technical solutions and does not comply with the provisions of Article 68 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (revised in 2002, hereinafter referred to as the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law). The Patent Reexamination Board's refusal to accept the amended text on the ground that it did not comply with the above provisions did not constitute an error in the application of law. During the oral hearing phase of the patent invalidation proceeding, Wansheng Company also agreed in court that the Patent Reexamination Board would not accept the text that was not a deletion of parallel technical solutions. With respect to the determination of inventiveness, Evidence 1 does not define or record the specific compound as described by Wansheng Company in which the substituents R1, R13, R2, R3, R6, R7, R8 are respectively "R1 represents an optionally substituted phenyl group connected at the 4-position, with the substitution site at the 5-position, R13 is a tetrazolyl group, R2 represents hydrogen, R3 represents hydrogen, R6 represents a straight-chain propyl group, R7 represents a branched-chain butyl group, R8 represents a carboxyl group." Therefore, the technical solution of the specific compound described by Wansheng Company was not disclosed in Evidence 1, and the inventiveness of claim 1 of the patent in question cannot be assessed on this basis. Compared with the second compound (i.e., the compound of Example 329 of Evidence 1) and the third compound (i.e., the compound of Example 265C of Evidence 1) among the preferred compounds referred to on page 15 of the Chinese translation of Evidence 1, the difference from claim 1 of the patent in question is that the substituents at the 4-position of the imidazole ring of the compounds of Examples 329 and 265C are C2F5 and COOH groups, respectively, while the substituent at the 4-position of the imidazole ring of the compound of claim 1 of the patent in question is R2R3(OR4) as defined in claim 1. These are clearly different. Therefore, Evidence 1 does not provide a technical teaching that the substituent at the 4-position of the imidazole ring could be a hydroxyl branched-chain alkyl group or an alkoxy branched-chain alkyl group. At the same time, Wansheng Company also did not provide prior art evidence to prove that the substituent at the 4-position of the imidazole ring of the compounds of Examples 329 and 265C could be replaced by a hydroxyl branched-chain alkyl group or an alkoxy branched-chain alkyl group and that such replacement would yield similar activity or effect. Furthermore, from the corresponding content recorded on page 2 of the specification, it cannot be concluded, as Wansheng Company argued, that "the AII receptor inhibitory activity is not significantly related to the substituents at other positions of the imidazole ring." With respect to the technical effect of the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent in question, pages 107-108 of the specification of the patent in question have recorded the activity data of a number of specific compounds of formula (I) as claimed in claim 1, which produce unexpected effects compared to compound A of the prior art. Therefore, claim 1 of the patent in question is non-obvious over Evidence 1 and possesses inventiveness as provided in Article 22, paragraph 3 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (implemented in 2001, hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law).

In summary, in accordance with Article 54, paragraph (1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered the judgment: upholding Decision No. 16266 made by the Patent Reexamination Board.

Wansheng Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court, requesting the reversal of the judgment of first instance and Decision No. 16266, and ordering the Patent Reexamination Board to make a new examination decision. The reasons were as follows: 1. The determination of the type of the invalidation decision in the judgment of first instance and Decision No. 16266 was erroneous; it should have been a partial invalidation of the patent right, not a maintenance of the patent right valid. 2. The determination in the judgment of first instance and Decision No. 16266 that the specific compound disclosed in Evidence 1 could not constitute the closest prior art solution for evaluating the inventiveness of the patent in question was erroneous. 3. The determination in the judgment of first instance and Decision No. 16266 that claim 1 of the patent in question possessed inventiveness compared to the compounds of Examples 329 and 265C of Evidence 1 was erroneous. 4. The Patent Reexamination Board's refusal to allow Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. to partially amend claim 1 of the patent in question constituted an improper application of law.

The Patent Reexamination Board and Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. adhered to the judgment of first instance.

The court of second instance held that: (I) With respect to whether there was an error in fact finding on the front page of Decision No. 16266. In this case, Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. voluntarily abandoned part of the technical solutions at the time of patent grant through a proactive amendment. The "Basis for Examination" section of the "Reasons for the Decision" in Decision No. 16266 has already made clear that the text on which the decision was based was claim 1 submitted by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. on January 14, 2011, rather than the claim text at the time of patent grant. The Patent Reexamination Board clearly stated in the main body of Decision No. 16266 that it maintained the patent right valid on the basis of the amended text submitted by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. on January 14, 2011. Therefore, as a whole, the designation of the type of the invalidation decision as "maintaining the patent right valid" on the front page of Decision No. 16266 should be understood as maintaining the patent right valid on the basis of the amended text submitted by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. on January 14, 2011, rather than maintaining the patent right valid on the basis of the claim text at the time of patent grant. Therefore, there is no error in fact finding in Decision No. 16266. Wansheng Company's appeal argument that there was an error in fact finding on the front page of Decision No. 16266 cannot be sustained. Of course, the Patent Reexamination Board may further improve the format of the front page of the invalidation decision by adding the content of maintaining the patent right valid on the basis of the amended text, thereby reducing misunderstandings arising from this.

(II) With respect to whether there was an error in the application of law by the Patent Reexamination Board in not allowing Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. to amend the claims. Article 68, paragraph 1 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law provides that during the examination of a request for invalidation, the patentee of an invention or utility model patent may amend its claims, but shall not expand the scope of protection of the original patent. The claim of the patent in question adopts the drafting method of a Markush claim. A Markush claim is a type of claim that defines multiple parallel optional elements in a single claim, specifically referring to a claim that includes multiple variables, each variable including multiple different options, characterized by the enumeration of parallel options to express the scope of protection of the claim. Therefore, when a Markush claim covers compounds, these compounds are in a parallel selection relationship, each compound is an independent technical solution, and the claim encompasses a collection of multiple technical solutions, where the elements can be substituted for each other to achieve the same effect. Since a Markush claim is considered a special type of parallel technical solution, and such deletion narrows the scope of protection of the patent right, complies with the provisions of Article 68, paragraph 1 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law, and does not harm the public interest, the patentee should be allowed to delete the relevant selection items. However, given that at the time of grant of a Markush claim, not all compounds covered by the claim are necessarily synthesized, the limit for allowing amendments is that the amended claim shall not become a specific compound not recorded in the specification; otherwise, it would undermine the basis for selection inventions directed to Markush claims.

The court of first instance and the Patent Reexamination Board both held that the deletion of Markush elements from a Markush claim does not directly equate to the deletion of parallel technical solutions and does not comply with the provisions of Article 68 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law. This view essentially regards a granted Markush claim as an integral technical solution and does not allow deletion. It is well known that in the drafting of patent documents and during patent examination, both patent applicants and examiners can only search the prior art within a limited scope. Given the breadth of the prior art, it is impossible for anyone to retrieve all prior art. If a granted Markush claim is regarded as an integral technical solution and deletion of any selection item of any variable is not permitted, the patent right obtained by the patentee would inevitably be vulnerable to invalidation challenges from others. The patentee cannot foresee whether a specific technical solution falling within the scope of the patent existed before the filing date, and thus the patent obtained could easily be declared invalid, depriving the so-called Markush claim of its raison d'être. Therefore, both in patent grant examination proceedings and in invalidation proceedings, patent applicants or patentees should be allowed to delete any selection item of any variable, and such deletion constitutes a deletion of a technical solution.

In this case, the amended text submitted by Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. on August 30, 2010 made the following amendments to claim 1: (1) deleted "or an ester" from "or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt or ester thereof" in claim 1; (2) deleted "an alkyl group having 1 to 6 carbon atoms" from the definition of R4 in claim 1; (3) deleted definitions other than carboxyl group and formula COOR5a (wherein R5a is (5-methyl-2-oxo-1,3-dioxolen-4-yl)methyl) from the definition of R5 in claim 1. The Patent Reexamination Board's refusal to allow the amendments in items (2) and (3) above deviated from the legislative intent of Article 68 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law, which was inappropriate. However, given that Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. did not raise any objection and the rights of Wansheng Company were not harmed, Wansheng Company's appeal argument that Decision No. 16266 violated Article 68 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law and should be revoked cannot be sustained and is not supported.

(III) With respect to whether claim 1 possesses inventiveness. Article 22, paragraph 3 of the Patent Law provides that inventiveness means that, compared with the prior art existing before the filing date, the invention has prominent substantive features and represents notable progress. It is well known that when a Markush claim covers compounds, the claim often encompasses thousands or even tens of thousands of specific compounds, with a relatively broad scope of protection. Each specific compound covered should have unexpected uses or effects compared with structurally similar specific compounds in the prior art. When assessing the inventiveness of Markush claims of different scopes, a certain screening should be conducted within the scope of the Markush claims of different ranges, selecting specific compounds as close as possible for comparison of technical effects. As long as at least one specific compound encompassed by the Markush claim does not have unexpected uses or effects compared with the technical effect of at least one specific compound in the prior art, then the Markush claim lacks inventiveness.

In this case, after screening the experimental compounds of the patent in question, Examples 10, 17, 19, 22-24, 50, and 69 were identified as specific examples for comparison with Example 329 of Evidence 1, which differs only by one substituent, in terms of ID50 data. Only four examples showed better effects than Example 329, while the other four showed significantly worse effects. This comparison result shows that the effect of one specific example encompassed by the claim of the patent in question is comparable to the technical effect of Example 329 of Evidence 1 in the prior art. Therefore, claim 1 of the patent in question has not achieved unexpected technical effects and lacks inventiveness. Wansheng Company's appeal argument that claim 1 of the patent in question lacks inventiveness is sustained, and this court supports it.

Given that Decision No. 16266 only assessed and decided on the inventiveness of claim 1 of the patent in question and did not examine the other dependent claims, the Patent Reexamination Board should, on the basis that claim 1 of the patent in question lacks inventiveness, continue to examine the other claims and make a new decision.

In summary, the judgment of first instance and Decision No. 16266 were based on unclear facts and erroneous application of law and should be revoked. Part of Wansheng Company's appeal arguments are sustained, and its appeal requests should be supported. In accordance with Article 61, paragraph (3) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 70 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of second instance rendered the judgment: (1) Revoke the administrative judgment (2011) Yizhong Zhixing Chu Zi No. 2403 of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court of the People's Republic of China; (2) Revoke Decision No. 16266 on the Request for Invalidation issued by the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China; (3) The Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China shall make a new invalidation decision regarding the invention patent with patent number 97126347.7, titled "Method for preparing a pharmaceutical composition for treating or preventing hypertension." The first-instance and second-instance case acceptance fees, each RMB 100, shall be borne by the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China (to be paid within seven days from the effective date of this judgment).

The Patent Reexamination Board applied for retrial, arguing: (I) The judgment of second instance erred in determining the legal nature of Markush claims. 1. With respect to compounds of a general formula, a compound claim drafted in Markush form constitutes a generic technical solution and should not be simply regarded as a collection of numerous compounds. 2. The enumeration of numerous variables and their many optional items in a Markush general formula cannot be equated to the Markush claim being considered as clearly defined and independent specific compound technical solutions. 3. Treating a Markush claim as a clear and independent set of specific compounds departs from the original intent of protecting Markush compounds. The fundamental purpose of a patent applicant drafting claims in Markush form at the time of application is to maximize the scope of protection around similar compounds, while also drafting dependent claims to protect the core compounds it has already implemented. The judgment of second instance isolatedly understood the Markush compound as part of the claim set, ignoring the fact that it is not the entirety. 4. The objective fact that Markush compounds themselves expand in a multi-level, branching manner cannot be accurately represented by a model of specific compounds in a parallel collection (like ping-pong balls in a container). (II) The judgment of second instance's view that any selection item of any variable in a Markush claim can be deleted, that narrowing the scope is not deemed to harm the public interest, and that the limit for allowing amendments is that no specific compound not recorded in the specification may appear, is erroneous. 1. The arbitrary deletion of any variable and any selection item inevitably creates "brand new" "narrowed" intermediate scopes of protection, which does not comply with the relevant provisions of the Patent Law. 2. Currently, there is no limit on the number of claims after amendment in invalidation proceedings. If arbitrary deletion is allowed, the patentee could construct new intermediate-scope Markush claims by deleting different levels or numbers of variables or options. 3. If deletion of any selection item of any variable in a Markush general formula is allowed, the patentee could also add as new claims all "specific compounds" mentioned in the specification but never claimed in the granted claims. These new claims for specific compounds might only be table compounds in the specification, which would seriously affect the public's reliance interest in the granted patent. 4. Although deleting a variable results in a new intermediate-scope claim that narrows the protection scope relative to one granted Markush claim, the number of new intermediate-scope claims added in invalidation proceedings may far exceed the original one granted Markush claim. As a result, through the invalidation proceeding, the patentee could construct a closer new prior art through its new claims, increasing the difficulty for subsequent selection inventions, deviating from the assumption that narrowing the scope would benefit the public interest. 5. At the grant stage, although the patentee implemented only a limited number of specific compounds, by leveraging modern chemical technology and techniques such as data simulation, and based on the prior art, it sought protection for a large number of similar compounds. Allowing amendments of any selection item of any variable effectively provides guidance that a Markush compound can be sufficiently protected with just one claim in a patent application, and then through amendments in invalidation proceedings, many different scopes of technical solutions, or even technical solutions for certain specific compounds, can be obtained. (III) The judgment of second instance erroneously assessed the inventiveness of the involved application. 1. The decision under review did not involve a factual error of selecting non-close specific compounds. The different-scope Markush compounds in Decision No. 16266 were invalidation grounds repeatedly emphasized by the requester in the invalidation proceeding and were issues that the invalidation proceeding had to respond to and determine. 2. In the determination of inventiveness, the assessment of non-obviousness and unexpected technical effect should be organically unified. Whether an unexpected technical effect is produced should not be a standalone factor in the inventiveness determination; rather, it should be inherent in the process of determining the technical problem actually solved by the invention and the technical teaching, embedded in the assessment of non-obviousness, or used as a supplementary consideration to weigh whether the technical contribution made by the inventor matches the protection obtained, after a preliminary determination of non-obviousness. 3. Evidence 1 shows that the substituents at the 4-position of the imidazole ring can be various, and it does not even record that the 4-position of the imidazole ring of the general formula compounds in this patent can be replaced by the broader substituent type of "hydroxyl branched-chain alkyl or alkoxy branched-chain alkyl." From this, it can be seen that regardless of how the substituents at the 4-position of the imidazole ring in the general formula compounds of Evidence 1 are selected, there is no motivation to select the substituent at the 4-position of the imidazole ring as in claim 1 of this patent. Evidence 1 does not disclose, and the requester has not provided evidence to prove, that the alkyl group at the 4-position of the imidazole ring in the compounds of formula 1 of Evidence 1 can be mutually substituted with a hydroxyl branched-chain alkyl or alkoxy branched-chain alkyl group, nor does it disclose that the effects of such mutual substitution are the same or similar. Claim 1 is non-obvious over Evidence 1. (IV) The judgment of second instance introduced the effect data of compounds 10, 17, 50, and 69 on its own, which were not involved in the decision under review or the judgment of first instance. This constitutes new facts and violates the Administrative Procedure Law. Therefore, it requested the revocation of the judgment of second instance and the maintenance of the decision under review.

Wansheng Company argued in its response that: (1) The second-instance judgment's determination regarding the method of amending the Markush claim was correct. 1. A Markush compound claim should be understood as a collection of parallel technical solutions, not an indivisible overall technical solution. The Patent Reexamination Board's refusal to accept the amended text submitted by the patentee on August 30, 2010, had no legal basis or practical foundation. 2. In judicial practice, for general formula compound claims drafted in Markush form, when it is challenged that the scope of generalization is too broad and lacks support from the specification, or when it is challenged that the claim encompasses a compound disclosed in the prior art and thus lacks novelty, such issues arise. 3. The Patent Reexamination Board's approach of allowing deletion of "or ester" but not allowing deletion of the groups that could be selected from substituents R4 and R5 in the general formula I compound was logically contradictory. 4. In the invalidation procedure, narrowing the scope of patent protection is a right conferred on the patentee by law, and the patentee does not gain any benefit from doing so. This right should not be deprived simply because the claim is drafted in Markush form. 5. From the perspective of balancing the interests of the patentee and the public, there is no reason in the invalidation procedure to prohibit deleting parallel selectable groups from a Markush general formula claim. 6. The invalidation decision, based on an erroneous examination text, violated procedural fairness and should be revoked. (2) Claim 1 of the patent lacked inventiveness. For a general formula compound of a Markush claim, the closest prior art should be a known compound that is structurally closest and has the best effect compared to the claimed compound. Only when all parallel technical solutions encompassed in the Markush claim, at least all specifically implemented inventive compounds (which form the basis of support for the Markush claim), achieve unexpected uses and effects compared to the closest prior art, can the Markush claim be considered inventive. In this case, the compound of Example 329 and the compound of Example 265c of Evidence 1 were structurally close to the compounds of the patent. The general formula compound of Markush claim 1 of the patent, in addition to containing the eight example compounds of the patent that underwent activity tests and their equivalent alternatives or obvious variants, actually encompassed a vast number of other compounds whose activity effects were not experimentally verified in the patent document. Therefore, it could not be demonstrated that they achieved unexpected effects. The generalized Markush claim 1 of the patent could not satisfy the requirement of achieving unexpected uses or effects compared to the closest prior art compound disclosed in Evidence 1. Hence, claim 1 of the patent lacked inventiveness. (3) The Patent Reexamination Board argued that the second-instance judgment introduced new facts unfavorable to the patentee (i.e., the effect data of compounds 10, 17, 50, and 69). Wansheng Company did not agree with this. The effect data of the above example compounds were recorded in the granted specification of the patent. Wansheng Company had mentioned and commented on the above examples in the administrative complaint submitted in the first-instance proceedings and during the first-instance trial. In the first-instance proceedings, both Wansheng Company and the Patent Reexamination Board recognized and used the unilateral experimental data submitted by the patentee to evaluate the inventiveness of the patent. Therefore, Wansheng Company requested that the retrial petition of the Patent Reexamination Board be dismissed and the second-instance judgment be upheld.

Daiichi Sankyo Co., Ltd. submitted its opinion that: (1) Chapter 10 of Part Two of the Patent Examination Guidelines stipulates that if an application defines multiple parallel selectable elements in one claim, it constitutes a Markush claim. Based on the above definition, different substituents in a Markush claim are parallel selectable elements and should therefore be considered parallel technical solutions, allowing deletion during the invalidation procedure. The principle for amending during the invalidation procedure, i.e., whether it exceeds the scope of protection of the original specification, should be strictly applied to prevent harm to public interests in the invalidation procedure. However, the method of amendment during the invalidation procedure should not be overly strict or harsh. As long as it does not impair the public notice effect of the original claim and remains within the foreseeable scope of the public, it should be permitted. (2) The second-instance judgment's determination that the patent lacked inventiveness was erroneous. 1. The second-instance judgment ignored the fact that the patent was an improvement specifically directed to Evidence 1. 2. Compared with Example 329 of Evidence 1, among the four inventive compounds (Examples 10, 17, 23, and 50) that showed deteriorated effects, at least three different substituents were involved, whereas the second-instance judgment found that only one substituent differed. 3. The second-instance judgment applied the law incorrectly. According to Chapter 10 of Part Two of the Patent Examination Guidelines, a compound structurally close to a known compound must have unexpected technical effects. All compounds within the scope of protection of a Markush claim should be compared with all "close compounds" of that compound, not with all compounds of the prior art, to determine unexpected technical effects. Therefore, Daiichi Sankyo requested that the case be retried and the judgment be modified to support its claims.

This Court holds that the issues in dispute are: (1) Whether a compound claim drafted in Markush form is a generalized technical solution or a collection of numerous compounds; (2) In the invalidation stage, what method can the patentee use to amend a Markush claim; (3) Whether claim 1 of the patent application possesses inventiveness.

(1) Regarding whether a compound claim drafted in Markush form is a generalized technical solution or a collection of numerous compounds

Article 31, paragraph 1 of the Patent Law provides: "An application for a patent for invention or utility model shall be limited to one invention or utility model. Two or more inventions or utility models belonging to a single general inventive concept may be filed as one application." Article 34 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law provides: "Two or more inventions or utility models that may be filed as one patent application in accordance with Article 31, paragraph 1 of the Patent Law shall be technically interrelated and contain one or more same or corresponding specific technical features, where 'specific technical features' refer to the technical features that each invention or utility model, as a whole, contributes to the prior art." A Markush claim is a special way of drafting claims in chemical invention patent applications, i.e., a claim that defines multiple parallel selectable elements in one application. The Markush claim drafting method was created to address the problem that in the chemical field, multiple substituent groups cannot be generalized under a common superordinate concept. It has itself always been regarded as a structural expression, not a functional expression. A Markush claim defines parallel selectable elements, not claims. All selectable compounds have common properties and functions and share a common structure, or all selectable elements belong to a recognized same class of compounds in the field of the invention. Although Markush claims are drafted in a special way, they must still comply with the provisions of the Patent Law and its Implementing Regulations on unity of invention.

A Markush claim has a strong generalization ability. Once granted, the scope of patent protection will cover all compounds with the same structure, properties, or functions, maximizing the interests of the patentee. In essence, a patent is a monopoly over a certain right. The broader the scope of rights enjoyed by the patentee, the more limitations imposed on the public. Therefore, from the perspective of fairness, the interpretation of Markush claims should be strict. Regardless of how many variables and combinations a Markush claim contains, it should be regarded as a generalized combination solution. Selecting one variable should generate a drug with the same effect, i.e., selecting different molecular formulas generates different drugs, but the efficacy of these drugs should not differ significantly; they should be interchangeable, and the expected effects should be the same. This aligns with the original purpose of creating Markush claims. Therefore, a Markush claim should be regarded as a collection of Markush elements, not a collection of numerous compounds. A Markush element only manifests as a single compound in specific circumstances, but generally, a Markush element should be understood as a class of compounds with common properties and functions. If a Markush claim is considered to describe numerous compounds, it would clearly violate the unity requirement. Hence, the second-instance judgment's view that a Markush claim constitutes parallel technical solutions was incorrect and should be corrected.

(2) Regarding what method the patentee can use to amend a Markush claim during the review stage of an invalidation request

The Patent Examination Guidelines (2010) stipulate that during the review stage of an invalidation request, amendments to the patent specification for invention or utility model patents shall be limited to the claims and follow these basic principles: 1. The title of the subject matter of the original claims shall not be changed; 2. Compared with the granted claims, the scope of protection shall not be expanded; 3. The technical features shall not go beyond those recorded in the original specification and claims; 4. Generally, technical features not included in the granted claims shall not be added. However, currently, the amendment method has been changed to, subject to the above amendment principles, the specific methods for amending claims are generally limited to deletion of claims, deletion of technical solutions, further limitation of claims, and correction of obvious errors. Further limitation of a claim means adding one or more technical features recorded in other claims to the claim to narrow the scope of protection. It can be seen that in the invalidation procedure, the methods for amending patent documents have become more diversified. However, there are many special issues in the examination of invention patent applications in the chemical field, such as whether a chemical invention can be implemented requires confirmation through experimental results; some chemical products need to be defined by parameters or preparation methods; new properties and uses of known chemical products do not necessarily imply changes in structure or composition, etc. Given the particularity of chemical inventions, and considering that at the time of drafting a Markush claim, the patent applicant had the opportunity to include all structural forms in one claim to obtain the maximum scope of protection, amendments to Markush claims during the invalidation stage must be strictly limited. The principle allowing amendments to Markush claims should be that the amendment cannot create a new class or single compound with new properties or functions, but individual circumstances must also be fully considered. If the patent applicant or patentee is allowed to delete any option of any variable, even if such deletion narrows the scope of protection and does not harm the rights of the public, the uncertainty as to whether a new scope of protection is created would not only fail to provide a stable expectation to the public but also undermine the stability of the patent confirmation system. Therefore, the relevant determination of the second-instance court was clearly inappropriate and is corrected by this Court.

(3) Regarding the determination of inventiveness of a Markush claim

The determination of inventiveness of a Markush claim should follow the basic method for determining inventiveness, i.e., the "three-step method" prescribed in the Patent Examination Guidelines. Unexpected technical effect is an auxiliary factor in determining inventiveness and, as a reverse inference method, is special and not universally applicable. Therefore, only when the examination and determination through the "three-step method" cannot conclude whether the invention is obvious or not, can unexpected technical effects be used to determine whether a patent application has inventiveness. Generally, it is not appropriate to skip the "three-step method" and directly apply unexpected technical effects to determine inventiveness.

Regarding the issue of comparison of technical effects, in this case, the Patent Reexamination Board did not compare Examples 10, 17, 50, and 69 of the comparison document with the examples of the patent in the invalidation procedure and make a determination. However, the second-instance court directly made the comparison and determination, which exceeded the scope of review of the invalidation decision and violated the provisions of the Administrative Procedure Law and relevant judicial interpretations. This is corrected by this Court.

The requester for invalidation, Wansheng Company, argued that claim 1 of the patent lacked inventiveness and cited Evidence 1 as the closest prior art. When determining the inventiveness of claim 1 of the patent, the Patent Reexamination Board and the first-instance court strictly followed the "three-step method," determined that the compound of formula I in claim 1 differed from the compound of formula I in Evidence 1 by two distinguishing technical features, and then analyzed the non-obviousness of the two distinguishing technical features, thereby concluding that claim 1 of the patent was inventive. This was not improper. Accordingly, the Patent Reexamination Board's ground for retrial was established and is supported by this Court.

In summary, the retrial petition of the Patent Reexamination Board meets the circumstances provided in Article 91 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 89, paragraph 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 76 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. The administrative judgment (2012) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 833 of the Beijing High People's Court of the People's Republic of China is reversed;

2. The administrative judgment (2011) Yi Zhong Zhi Xing Chu Zi No. 2403 of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court of the People's Republic of China is affirmed.

The court acceptance fees for the first and second instances, each RMB 100, shall be borne by Beijing Wansheng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (both to be paid within seven days from the date this judgment takes effect).

This judgment is final.
